title: Bohus-inspired mini scarf
subtitle: A short neckwarmer with a stranded colourwork yoke inspired by Swedish Bohus knitting.
excerpt: A short mini scarf knitted flat in two-colour stranded colourwork on 3.75 mm needles with fingering-weight yarn, finishing at 16 cm wide by 55 cm long. The colourwork panel runs the full width of the scarf for 30 rows in the centre of the length, worked from a 12-stitch by 30-row chart that echoes the angular purl-stitch bead technique of 1940s Bohus Stickning cooperatives.
sourceNotes: Bohus Stickning was a Swedish knitting cooperative (1939–1969) known for stranded colourwork with purl beads in the contrast colour. The technique is historically documented in Emma Jacobsson's designs and in the Gothenburg Museum collections. This chart is original and draws aesthetic inspiration from Bohus geometric patterns without reproducing any specific design.
heroPrompt: A finished Bohus-inspired mini scarf in pale grey fingering weight with a deep teal colourwork panel in the centre, showing the angular geometric pattern with purl bead highlights, photographed folded on a pale wooden surface.

chartDefinition.notes: Read RS rows right to left, WS rows left to right (flat knitting). On RS rows: . = MC knit, X = CC knit, P = CC purl (the Bohus bead). On WS rows: . = MC purl, X = CC purl, P = CC knit (reverse of RS because the bead must appear as a purl nub on the right side). Carry both yarns across every row; do not float more than 5 stitches without catching. Repeat the 12-stitch chart across the full 42-stitch width (3 full repeats + 6 stitches of border; see below).

glossaryTerms.definition: A purl stitch worked in the contrast colour on a right-side row, producing a raised nub of contrast colour that appears as a decorative dot or 'bead' in the colourwork pattern. Associated with the Swedish Bohus Stickning cooperative (1939–1969).
A technique in which two yarn colours are carried across every row. The yarn not currently in use is stranded (floated) across the wrong side of the work.
The length of yarn carried across the wrong side while the other colour is worked. Floats longer than 5 stitches should be caught on the wrong side to prevent snagging.
A cast-on forming a neat elastic edge by using the tail and working yarn over two fingers simultaneously.

content.text: This is a short mini scarf knitted flat in two-colour
stranded colourwork

on 3.75 mm needles with fingering-weight yarn, finishing at 16 cm wide and 55 cm long when blocked. The colourwork panel fills the centre 30 rows of the scarf and uses the angular purl-bead motif technique of the Swedish Bohus Stickning cooperative: contrast-colour stitches are occasionally purled on the right side to create raised bead nubs (
Bohus purl beads
) within the stranded pattern.

This is the most technically demanding pattern in the scarf-cowl collection. The Bohus purl bead requires working a purl stitch in the contrast yarn on a right-side row while both yarns are in the correct stranding position, then reversing the logic on the wrong-side row. Managing this alongside
float
tension across the flat rows places it firmly at ADVANCED level. The finished scarf needs about 200 m (approximately 65 g) of MC and 80 m (approximately 25 g) of CC in fingering-weight yarn.
What you need

items.name: Fingering-weight yarn, main colour (MC)
items.substitutions: Any smooth fingering-weight yarn. Wool or wool-blend gives the clearest stitch definition.

items.name: Fingering-weight yarn, contrast colour (CC)
items.substitutions: One or two contrast colours can be used; traditional Bohus used a light main with jewel-toned contrast.

items.name: 3.75 mm needles, straight or circular (UK 9 / US 5)

content.text: Gauge

26 sts x 34 rows = 10 x 10 cm in stocking stitch on 3.75 mm needles, blocked. In the stranded colourwork panel the row gauge is approximately 36 rows per 10 cm because the floats pull the fabric slightly shorter. Swatch the chart pattern and measure after blocking. One stitch per 10 cm off gauge shifts the finished width by approximately 0.6 cm at this stitch count.
Reading the chart and the purl bead

Read RS rows right to left, WS rows left to right. The chart is 12 stitches wide. For 42 stitches work: K3 MC border, then 3 full 12-stitch repeats (36 stitches), then K3 MC border. Borders are always worked in MC.

The P symbol in the chart means: on a RS row, bring the CC yarn to the front, purl 1 stitch in CC, return CC to back. The stitch will appear as a raised CC purl nub on the right side. On WS rows, a P symbol becomes a CC knit stitch (to create the same purl nub on the RS).
Pattern
Cast on
Use the
long-tail cast-on

in MC to place 42 stitches on the needle. Before beginning, calculate the tail: tail_cm = (needle circumference mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For 3.75 mm needles (circumference approximately 11.8 mm) and 42 stitches: (11.8 x 42) / 10 + 15 = 49.6 + 15 = about 65 cm. Leave at least 65 cm of MC tail.
Stitch count check-in: after the cast-on you should have 42 stitches on the needle.
Opening section (57 rows of plain stocking stitch in MC)
RS rows: K42. WS rows: P42. Work 57 rows total (approx. 16 cm). End on a WS row.
Colourwork panel (30 rows from chart)

Join CC at the right edge on a RS row. Work chart rows 1 to 30: K3 MC border, [12-stitch repeat × 3 times], K3 MC border. Maintain flat construction (RS rows read right to left; WS rows read left to right). Watch for P symbols and work them as CC purl on RS / CC knit on WS.
Stitch count check-in: at the halfway mark (approximately row 94 of the full body, which falls in the middle of the colourwork panel), you should have 42 stitches on the needle.
Closing section (73 rows of plain stocking stitch in MC)

Drop CC and continue in MC only. Work 73 rows (approx. 21 cm) of stocking stitch. The closing section is longer than the opening to compensate for the colourwork panel pulling in slightly. Bind off on a RS row.
Common faults

Purl bead not standing out. If the CC purl bead looks the same as the surrounding stitches, the CC yarn was not brought fully to the front before purling. The bead only stands proud if the CC is in front of the needle when the stitch is worked. Practice on a swatch before knitting the full panel.

Colourwork panel pulling in narrower than the plain sections. Floats in the panel are too tight. Before working each row of the chart, spread the stitches on the right needle to the full relaxed width of the scarf, then strand the float across. The floats must span the same width as the stitches.

Confusion about WS purl bead logic. On WS rows the chart P symbol means CC knit (not CC purl). This counterintuitive reversal is because WS rows are the mirror of RS rows. If you accidentally CC purl on a WS row instead of CC knitting, the bead will appear on the wrong side.
Finishing

Weave in all tails from MC and CC at the colourwork panel edges. Block thoroughly: soak in cool water for 20 minutes, press out water gently, pin to 16 x 55 cm on blocking mats. The colourwork panel must be pinned to the same width as the plain sections to align the scarf. Allow to dry fully before unpinning.
Care
Handwash in cool water with wool wash. Do not rub or wring. Reblock after washing to realign the colourwork panel with the plain sections.
What to try next

The Fair Isle scarf uses the same two-colour stranded technique across the full scarf length with a geometric repeat that has no purl beads. The lace stole is the other ADVANCED project in this collection, using a completely different technique.
